To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
contextual control, stimulus generalization and equivalence can be used to create a hierarchy of stimulus functions.

(a) contextual control over selection responses was established in a hierarchy of physical features, (b) the evocative function of these features generalized along the hierarchy, (c) these evocative functions were acquired by a set stimuli via transitivity relations, and (d) the stimuli acquired via transitivity relations served as names for stimulus classes within each hierarchy level.

contextual control of differential responding to specific stimulus features can be extended to other stimuli by stimulus generalization and that these generalized functions can be acquired by a set other stimuli by stimulus equivalence.

the role of context in the acquisition of hierarchical categorization.
how contextual control of stimulus functions can be used to establish stimulus equivalence relations.
how contextual control and stimulus equivalence interact in the development of hierarchical categorization.

stimulus generalization and equivalence were controlled by contextual stimuli.
the results of this experiment support the notion that stimulus generalization and equivalence relations can be used to create hierarchical categories.
contextual control of selection responses, generalization, and equivalence were all required for hierarchical categorization.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
contextual control of selection responses, stimulus generalization along a dimension, and stimulus equivalence can be combined to produce hierarchical categorization.
the contextual control of stimulus generalisation and stimulus equivalence is a viable alternative to the traditional method of stimulus equivalence training.

contextual control can be used to produce hierarchical categorization, which can then be used to acquire stimulus functions that generalize in predictable ways.
